opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is: more than most people expected two years ago, but less than the headlines suggest.

If you give a strong model a well-scoped direction, say "here's a known method, here's a benchmark, find a meaningful improvement," it can do a surprising amount of the pipeline end to end. It can read the related work, propose a few variants, write the training and evaluation code, run the experiments if you give it compute and a sandbox, make the plots, and draft a paper that reads like a normal ICLR submission. Some of these papers would plausibly get through review, especially in areas where the contribution is incremental and empirical.

But a few things are still weak. The first is taste: choosing a problem that actually matters. Models tend to drift toward safe, local improvements, the kind of paper reviewers call "solid but limited." The second is judgment about their own results. They often don't notice when a gain comes from a bug, an unfair baseline, or leakage, and they're too eager to tell a positive story. A good human researcher is paranoid about their own numbers; models aren't yet, unless you build that skepticism into the scaffolding. The third is long-horizon persistence. When the first three ideas fail, a strong PhD student reframes the whole problem. Models tend to keep tweaking hyperparameters.

So my rough picture is that AI can now produce a paper that clears the bar on form, and sometimes on substance, for the median accepted paper. But the papers that people still cite five years later, the ones that change how the field thinks, still mostly come from a human deciding what question is worth asking. The interesting shift is that the human's role is moving from "doing the work" to "deciding what's worth doing and checking whether it's real." That's also a bit uncomfortable for the review system, because review was built on the assumption that writing a polished paper is expensive, and that's no longer true.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could produce some papers that plausibly pass review if given compute and a sandbox, but it does not express the specific belief that eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs would enable an accepted paper by the ICLR submission deadline.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we have to separate two questions. One is whether AI can produce an artifact that gets past ICLR reviewers. The other is whether it can do the research. Those are not the same thing, and right now the gap between them is the whole story.

On the first question, honestly, the answer is already yes, at least sometimes. We've seen fully automated pipelines generate papers that got accepted at workshops, and I'd be surprised if there weren't main-track papers at the big conferences this year where the human contribution was mostly supervision. If you give a strong model a well-scoped problem, access to a GPU cluster, and a loop where it reads the literature, proposes a variant of an existing method, runs the ablations, and writes it up, the output can look very much like a median ICLR paper. The writing is clean, the related work section is thorough, the figures are fine. Reviewers are overloaded, and the review process is not designed to detect "competent but hollow."

But that's actually an indictment of the review process more than a compliment to the AI. A lot of accepted papers are incremental. They take a known technique, apply it to a new setting, show a two-point improvement on three benchmarks, and tell a plausible story. That genre is almost perfectly suited to what current models do well, which is pattern-matching on the structure of prior work and executing well-defined experiments without getting bored.

Where I think AI still falls short is in taste. Picking the right problem. Knowing which result is surprising versus which one is a trivial consequence of the setup. Noticing that your baseline is misconfigured and that's why the gains look good. Having the discipline to kill a project when the early signal is weak instead of torturing the experiments until something comes out positive. Models are, if anything, worse than humans at that last one, because they're very good at producing a convincing narrative for whatever numbers they got.

There's also the problem that the model doesn't really have a reason to care whether the finding is true. A grad student who publishes something wrong eventually pays for it. The model doesn't. So in automated pipelines you see this drift toward results that are technically reproducible but scientifically not very meaningful. Everything checks out and nothing matters.

So if you ask me what AI can do today, I'd say it can function as an extremely capable research engineer and a decent first-draft writer, and under a human who knows what the interesting question is, that combination can absolutely produce an ICLR paper, probably faster than most labs produce them now. What it can't yet do reliably is originate the idea that makes a paper worth reading five years later. And I think the field should be a little worried about the fact that the conference acceptance bar doesn't distinguish between those two things very well.

r001.rationale: The response says AI with access to a GPU cluster can help produce an ICLR paper under human guidance, but it does not specify eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs or producing an accepted paper by the submission deadline.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate producing a paper that looks like an ICLR submission from doing research that deserves acceptance. AI is already quite useful for the first part: organizing an argument, writing code, and drafting the paper. The harder part is finding a meaningful question, designing experiments that actually test the idea, and knowing what to do when the results contradict your hypothesis.

If a researcher provides the direction and keeps checking the work, I think AI can contribute substantially to a paper that gets accepted. If you mean giving it one instruction—“Go produce an ICLR paper”—and leaving it to choose the problem, run everything, and validate its own conclusions, I wouldn’t confidently say it can do that reliably.

And acceptance itself is a noisy measure. I’d be more interested in whether it produces a result that holds up when someone else checks it. That’s a stronger demonstration than a convincing manuscript.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI can contribute substantially when a researcher provides direction and checks the work, but does not express the specific belief that AI with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs can produce an accepted ICLR paper by the submission deadline.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can already help produce an ICLR-level paper, but that’s different from saying you can give it one instruction and reliably get an accepted paper back. It can help formulate a hypothesis, write code, run experiments, analyze results, and draft the paper. The difficult part is connecting those steps: choosing a question that matters, noticing when an experiment undermines the idea, and deciding what to try next.

If a researcher supplies the central insight and keeps correcting the direction, AI can do a substantial amount of the work. If you ask it to do everything autonomously, I’d expect much less reliable results. It might produce something that looks like a paper, but whether the contribution is novel and the evidence actually supports it requires much more scrutiny.

So my answer would depend on the conditions: how much human input it gets, how much compute it can use, and how many attempts it has. Getting one paper accepted after many attempts is a very different achievement from consistently doing good research.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help produce an ICLR-level paper, but does not express belief that it can produce an accepted paper by the submission deadline with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
